props.title: Lady Frankenstein

sections.content: Lady Frankenstein stands as a fascinating gender-flipped take on Mary Shelley's classic tale, arriving during horror cinema's exploitation heyday. Director Mel Welles and star Rosalba Neri (as Sara Frankenstein) deliver a pulpy but compelling story about Baron Frankenstein's daughter continuing her father's experiments. Like Daughters of Darkness (1971) and The Blood Spattered Bride (1972), it represents a wave of European horror films featuring powerful, morally ambiguous female protagonists who challenge genre conventions.

sections.content: The film cleverly subverts the traditional Frankenstein narrative by making Sara both creator and romantic interest. Unlike The Bride of Frankenstein (1935), where the female monster is purely an object, Sara actively drives the story through her scientific ambition and sexual agency. The film's blend of gothic horror and exploitation elements mirrors contemporary works like Vampyros Lesbos (1971) and The Blood on Satan's Claw (1971), reflecting changing attitudes about gender and power in early 70s horror.

While the production values don't match Universal's classic monster films, Lady Frankenstein compensates with atmospheric Italian Gothic styling reminiscent of Mario Bava's Black Sunday (1960) and Blood and Black Lace (1964). The castle laboratory scenes particularly showcase the film's ability to create memorable visuals on a modest budget, while Joseph Cotten adds legitimacy to the proceedings as Sara's doomed father. SUBHEAD: Gender and Science in Gothic Horror

sections.content: Lady Frankenstein shares DNA with other female-centered scientific horror films like The Wasp Woman (1959) and Dr. Jekyll and Sister Hyde (1971). These films explore anxieties about women in traditionally male domains while simultaneously empowering their protagonists through forbidden knowledge. Sara's determination to perfect her father's work, regardless of moral cost, challenges period assumptions about feminine virtue and scientific authority.
